questions.q: When a research scientist asks to "quickly try X," what does "quick" usually refer to, according to the lesson?
options: Always a request for a fully rigorous, multi-seed experiment
The exact number of hours the implementation will take to build
The number of GPUs available on the cluster
The conceptual simplicity of the idea itself, not necessarily the engineering effort needed to test it rigorously at the required scale
questions.explain: A one-sentence idea can require real infrastructure work (seeds, baselines, logging, sweeps) to test rigorously that the simple description doesn't hint at -- the scientist's 'quick' refers to the idea's simplicity, not the implementation effort.

questions.q: What is one of the highest-value things an engineer does when a scientist brings a question like "does more data help here" instead of a fully specified experiment?
options: Telling the scientist to come back with a fully specified design before any work begins
Immediately running the experiment with whatever defaults are convenient
Ignoring the question until a formal ticket is filed
Filling in the unspecified details -- what must be held fixed, what confounds would make the result uninterpretable, and the minimum viable version that still gives a defensible answer
questions.explain: Translating a scientific question into a well-defined experiment -- identifying controls, confounds, and a minimum viable version -- is described as one of the highest-value contributions an engineer makes in this partnership.

questions.q: According to the lesson, when is it appropriate to push back on a scientist's requested experiment before building it?
options: Whenever the experiment would take more than one day to build
When the request has an obvious confound, such as comparing two models trained for different numbers of steps and attributing the difference to architecture alone
Only when the scientist explicitly asks for feedback
Never -- all requests should be implemented exactly as specified without comment
questions.explain: An obvious confound that would make the result ambiguous is worth raising before building, not after the run finishes. But the lesson warns against the opposite extreme of insisting on full rigor before any rough version is tried.

questions.q: Why might a rough, one-seed version of an experiment be a reasonable first step rather than insisting on full rigor immediately?
options: Because one seed is always sufficient to draw a final conclusion
Because it can cheaply answer whether an idea is even in the right neighborhood before investing in a fully rigorous, multi-seed version
Because rough versions are always more scientifically valid than rigorous ones
Because rigorous versions can never be built after a rough version
questions.explain: A scrappy, known-to-be-imperfect run can quickly tell whether an idea is promising enough to justify the larger investment of a rigorous, properly-seeded and logged experiment.

questions.q: What specific value does the lesson say a dedicated engineer typically adds that a scientist working alone usually can't match as fast?
options: Coming up with the original research hypothesis
Deciding which papers are worth reading
Writing the single training loop for the main experiment
Building the infrastructure (config systems, sweep tooling, cluster scheduling) that makes running many experiment variants with proper tracking and reproducibility as cheap as running one
questions.explain: The lesson frames infrastructure leverage -- making many variants cheap and reproducible to run -- as the engineer's distinct, high-value contribution, not a lesser supporting role relative to the scientist's research ideas.
